docs.title: pycopula-ml
docs.text:
pycopula-ml is a Python library for bivariate copula modeling, statistical dependence analysis, and graph construction. Its components can be used to develop probabilistic classification pipelines with continuous features.

The current package provides copula families, marginal distributions, parameter estimation, model selection, mutual information, and graph-building utilities. It does not expose a complete fit() / predict() classifier or train a neural network.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Six bivariate copula families: Frank, Clayton, Gaussian, Joe, Gumbel-Hougaard, and Ali-Mikhail-Haq.
  • Marginal transformations: continuous parametric marginals, empirical marginals, rank-based pseudo-observations, and candidate selection.
  • Parameter estimation: bounded maximum likelihood, including disjoint search intervals.
  • Model selection: AIC and BIC for fitted copula candidates.
  • Dependence analysis: copula-based mutual information and pairwise dependence matrices.
  • Graph construction: maximum-mutual-information spanning trees (MST) and heuristic maximum-mutual-information chains.

docs.title: Statistical workflow
docs.text:
For a feature pair \((X,Y)\), marginal transforms produce uniform pseudo-observations \((U,V)\). A bivariate copula is then fitted by maximizing

\[ \widehat\theta = \operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log c_\theta(u_i,v_i). \]

A fitted copula also provides model-based mutual information:

\[ I_C(X;Y) = \int_0^1\!\int_0^1 c(u,v)\log c(u,v)\,du\,dv. \]

For multiple features, pairwise estimates yield a dependence matrix that can be used to construct an MST or a chain. When fitting models per class, only training observations from that class should be used.

docs.title: pdf(u, v)
docs.text:
Evaluate

\[ c(u,v) = \frac{\partial^2C(u,v)} {\partial u\,\partial v}. \]

Subclasses must implement this method.

docs.title: logpdf(u, v)
docs.text:
Evaluate

\[ \log c(u,v). \]

The base implementation may use np.log(pdf()).

A subclass can override it with a numerically stable analytical expression.

docs.title: log_likelihood(u, v)
docs.text:
Evaluate the sample copula log-likelihood

\[ \ell = \sum_i\log c(u_i,v_i). \]

This method evaluates the likelihood at the parameter already stored in the copula instance.

Parameter search itself belongs to pycopula_ml.estimation.

docs.title: Other parametric copula families
docs.text:
In addition to Frank, the package documents Clayton, Gaussian, Joe, Gumbel-Hougaard, and Ali-Mikhail-Haq copulas. They follow the same BivariateCopula interface while imposing family-specific parameter domains and formulas.

See the parametric copulas overview and individual family pages for details.

A fitted bivariate copula can also be passed to mutual_information(). The dependence layer is separate from the copula density implementations and from parameter estimation.

docs.title: Example: known parameter
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from pycopula_ml.copulas import FrankCopula


u = np.array([0.2, 0.4, 0.7])
v = np.array([0.3, 0.6, 0.8])

copula = FrankCopula(theta=2.0)

print(copula.cdf(u, v))
print(copula.pdf(u, v))
print(copula.logpdf(u, v))
print(copula.log_likelihood(u, v))

docs.title: Example: unknown parameter
docs.text:
Use the estimation API rather than placing optimization logic inside the copula class:

from pycopula_ml.copulas import FrankCopula
from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle


result = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(
        (-50.0, -1e-6),
        (1e-6, 50.0),
    ),
)

copula = FrankCopula(theta=result.theta)

See Estimation API.

docs.title: gaussian_mutual_information(rho)
docs.text:
gaussian_mutual_information(rho: float) -> float

Return the exact mutual information (in nats) for a bivariate Gaussian copula:

\[ I=-\tfrac{1}{2}\log(1-\rho^2),\qquad -1<\rho<1. \]

Parameters

  • rho: finite Gaussian copula correlation, strictly between -1 and 1.

Returns: Python float, in nats.

Raises: ValueError for a nonfinite or out-of-domain rho.

docs.title: mutual_information(copula, *, order=64)
docs.text:
mutual_information(copula: object, *, order: int = 64) -> float

Evaluate the copula-based mutual information of an already instantiated continuous bivariate copula. Gaussian copulas use the closed-form expression; other copulas use tensor-product Gauss--Legendre quadrature over \((0,1)^2\).

Parameters

  • copula: fitted bivariate copula object exposing logpdf(u, v). Instances of GaussianCopula also provide theta, interpreted as rho.
  • order: integer quadrature order per dimension (minimum 8 in the numerical branch, default 64). Ignored for Gaussian copula evaluation.

Returns: Python float, in nats.

Raises:

  • ValueError: unsupported numerical quadrature order, incompatible log-density output shape, or materially negative numerical integral.
  • FloatingPointError: nonfinite or overflowing values in the quadrature computation.
from pycopula_ml.copulas.parametrics.frank import FrankCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import mutual_information

copula = FrankCopula(theta=3.0)
mi = mutual_information(copula, order=64)

docs.title: build_weight_matrices(...)
docs.text:
build_weight_matrices(
    U,
    copula_class,
    *,
    bounds,
    weight_method="mutual_information",
    feature_names=None,
    quadrature_order=64,
) -> CopulaWeightMatrices

Fit the chosen parametric bivariate copula to each pair of columns in the already transformed matrix U. Return a symmetric matrix for each of copula parameters, maximized log-likelihood, and mutual information.

Parameters

  • U: 2D array of shape (n_observations, n_features) with at least two observations and two features; finite values in the open interval (0,1).
  • copula_class: class or factory accepting theta=<candidate> and providing log_likelihood(u,v) and logpdf(u,v).
  • bounds: required bounded search interval or sequence of disjoint intervals accepted by fit_copula_mle().
  • weight_method: either "mutual_information" (default) or "likelihood".
  • feature_names: optional sequence of unique feature names; inferred from U.columns for DataFrames, otherwise generated as X1, X2, etc.
  • quadrature_order: integration order forwarded to mutual_information().

Returns: CopulaWeightMatrices.

Raises: ValueError for invalid data or configuration; RuntimeError if pairwise MLE fails; other numerical exceptions may propagate from fitting or integration.

docs.title: CopulaWeightMatrices
docs.text:
Frozen dataclass with attributes:

theta               : numpy.ndarray, shape (d, d)
log_likelihood      : numpy.ndarray, shape (d, d)
mutual_information  : numpy.ndarray, shape (d, d)
weights             : numpy.ndarray, shape (d, d)
feature_names       : tuple[str, ...]
weight_method       : str

All numeric matrices are symmetric and have a zero diagonal by construction. The diagonal is a placeholder, not the MI of a variable with itself. Although the dataclass is frozen, contained NumPy arrays may still be modified by callers.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from scipy.stats import rankdata
from pycopula_ml.copulas.parametrics.gaussian import GaussianCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import build_weight_matrices

# x: array of shape (n_observations, n_features)
u = rankdata(x, axis=0, method="average") / (len(x) + 1)

result = build_weight_matrices(
    u,
    GaussianCopula,
    bounds=(-0.95, 0.95),
)

print(result.mutual_information)

See Copula-based mutual information and Pairwise copula weight matrices for additional theory and statistical interpretation.

docs.title: build_chain_graph()
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.graphs import build_chain_graph

build_chain_graph(
    mi_matrix,
    *,
    method="best",
    feature_names=None,
) -> ChainGraph
  • mi_matrix: (d,d) symmetric MI matrix or CopulaWeightMatrices.
  • method: "greedy", "tsp", or "best".
  • feature_names: unique nonempty labels. If None, infer names from CopulaWeightMatrices, otherwise use X1, X2, ... .
  • Returns an immutable-result ChainGraph object. Its returned NumPy arrays are new allocations.
  • Raises ValueError for invalid method, dimensions, symmetry, negativity, diagonal, non-finite values, or names.

The score is in nats. No method guarantees a globally optimal Hamiltonian path. For mathematical details, read Chain graphs.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
The architecture separates six responsibilities:

  1. marginal modeling;
  2. dependence modeling with copulas;
  3. parameter estimation;
  4. dependence measures and pairwise weight matrices;
  5. graph construction from pairwise MI;
  6. future classification layers.

The package is organized into independent domains:

src/pycopula_ml/
├── copulas/
│   ├── base.py
│   └── parametrics/
│       ├── base.py
│       ├── frank.py
│       ├── clayton.py
│       ├── gaussian.py
│       ├── joe.py
│       ├── gumbel.py
│       └── ali_mikhail_haq.py
├── estimation/
│   └── maximum_likelihood.py
├── marginals/
│   ├── base.py
│   ├── empirical.py
│   ├── parametric.py
│   ├── result.py
│   └── selection.py
├── model_selection/
│   ├── copula_selector.py
│   └── criteria.py
├── dependence/
│   ├── mutual_information.py
│   └── weight_matrix.py
└── graphs/
    ├── __init__.py
    └── chain.py

docs.title: Statistical flow
docs.text:
For two original variables \(X\) and \(Y\),

\[ X \rightarrow \widehat F_X \rightarrow U, \] \[ Y \rightarrow \widehat F_Y \rightarrow V. \]

The dependence model then evaluates

\[ (U,V,\theta) \rightarrow C_\theta(U,V). \]

If \(\theta\) is unknown, the estimation layer uses the sample log-likelihood

\[ \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log c_\theta(u_i,v_i) \]

to obtain

\[ \widehat{\theta} = \operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta} \ell(\theta). \]

The full fitting workflow is therefore

original data
    ↓
marginal transformation
    ↓
pseudo-observations (u, v)
    ↓
copula log-likelihood
    ↓
parameter estimation
    ↓
theta_hat

This separation is deliberate.

A copula should not need to know whether \(U\) and \(V\) came from:

  • a Normal marginal;
  • a Gamma marginal;
  • a Lognormal marginal;
  • an empirical CDF;
  • rank-based pseudo-observations.

Likewise, the estimation layer should not contain the analytical density formula for every copula family. It operates through the common copula interface.

docs.title: Copula hierarchy
docs.text:
BivariateCopula
└── Parametric bivariate copulas
    ├── FrankCopula
    ├── ClaytonCopula
    ├── GaussianCopula
    ├── JoeCopula
    ├── GumbelCopula
    └── AliMikhailHaqCopula

The concrete class names and available exports depend on the active source version. All supported bivariate copulas share a common interface:

  • cdf();
  • pdf();
  • logpdf();
  • log_likelihood();
  • common input preparation and validation.

The family-specific subclasses provide their probability formulas and parameter restrictions.

docs.title: Marginal hierarchy
docs.text:
MarginalModel
├── EmpiricalMarginal
└── ContinuousMarginalModel
    └── ParametricMarginal

MarginalModel defines:

  • fit()
  • cdf()
  • transform()

ContinuousMarginalModel additionally requires:

  • pdf()
  • logpdf()

This distinction matters because an empirical CDF is a step function and does not have an ordinary continuous density suitable for the same PDF interface.

docs.title: Model-selection layer
docs.text:
MarginalSelector
├── MarginalCandidate
├── ParametricMarginal
└── MarginalFitResult

MarginalSelector is responsible for:

  • fitting multiple candidate distributions;
  • recording failed candidates;
  • ranking successful candidates;
  • selecting by AIC, BIC, or KS statistic;
  • producing warnings;
  • transforming observations with the selected marginal.

docs.title: Estimation layer
docs.text:
fit_copula_mle()
└── CopulaFitResult

The estimation layer is responsible for:

  • validating pseudo-observations for likelihood evaluation;
  • evaluating candidate copula log-likelihoods;
  • minimizing the negative log-likelihood;
  • searching one or several bounded parameter intervals;
  • selecting the best successful solution;
  • returning statistical and numerical diagnostics.

It is intentionally generic with respect to the copula family.

The estimator requires a copula class or factory that can be called as

copula(theta=<candidate>)

and whose instances implement

log_likelihood(u, v)

This is why user code passes

FrankCopula

rather than an already instantiated

FrankCopula(theta=...)

to fit_copula_mle().

docs.title: Why estimation is not under tools
docs.text:
A generic package path such as

pycopula_ml.tools

does not communicate the statistical responsibility of the code.

Maximum-likelihood fitting belongs under

pycopula_ml.estimation

because it is part of the public statistical model-fitting API, not merely an internal utility.

This also leaves room for future estimators such as:

estimation/
├── maximum_likelihood.py
├── rank_based.py
└── ...

without mixing statistical estimation with unrelated helpers.

docs.title: Dependence layer
docs.text:
The pycopula_ml.dependence layer consumes existing fitted copulas and MLE results; it does not reimplement their density formulas or numerical optimization.

Original feature matrix
          ↓
Rank-based pseudo-observations U
          ↓
Pairwise fit_copula_mle()
          ↓
Fitted copula for each feature pair
          ↓
mutual_information()
          ↓
CopulaWeightMatrices (L, Theta, M, weights)

For supervised classification, this process is repeated for each class, using only its training observations. The returned matrices describe pairwise dependence between features. Maximum-spanning trees, conditional class scoring, and GNN architectures are not implemented by this layer.

The Gaussian mutual-information branch uses a closed-form expression, while other continuous copulas use numerical quadrature. See Copula-based mutual information and Weight matrices.

docs.title: Design rule
docs.text:
The classifier planned for later should not contain logic such as:

if family == "frank":
    ...
elif family == "clayton":
    ...

It should operate through a common copula interface.

Similarly:

  • the copula layer should not decide which marginal distribution produced \(U\) and \(V\);
  • the estimation layer should not reimplement family-specific copula mathematics;
  • user scripts should not depend directly on the SciPy optimization backend.

docs.title: Separation of calculation and presentation
docs.text:
Core statistical classes and functions return values and structured results.

They should not depend on:

  • rich;
  • terminal formatting;
  • plotting;
  • interactive input.

Presentation utilities can be added separately later.

This keeps the statistical core usable from scripts, notebooks, tests, services, and future classifier components.

docs.title: Graph-construction layer
docs.text:
graphs.chain.build_chain_graph() consumes a mutual-information matrix or CopulaWeightMatrices from dependence. It does not fit copulas, marginal distributions, or a classifier. The output ChainGraph provides the ordered vertex permutation, named edges, total MI, weighted adjacency, and an optional bidirectional edge_index NumPy array for graph-learning pipelines.

The graph is a Hamiltonian path (one connected chain), not an unconstrained maximum spanning tree. Both provided algorithms are heuristics. A future classification module may use separate chains for each class, but such a classifier is not implemented by the current graph-construction API.

See Chain graphs.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The pycopula_ml.copulas package models dependence after marginal variables have been transformed to the unit interval.

For CDF and density evaluation, copula inputs belong to

\[ u,v\in[0,1]. \]

For parameter estimation through log-likelihood, the current estimation layer requires pseudo-observations strictly inside

\[ 0<u,v<1. \]

Original measurements \(X,Y\) should not be passed directly to a copula unless they are already uniform.

docs.title: BivariateCopula
docs.text:
The abstract base class defines a common interface for continuous bivariate copulas.

Required subclass implementations:

cdf(u, v)
pdf(u, v)

Default/common functionality:

logpdf(u, v)
log_likelihood(u, v)

The default logpdf() can be computed as

np.log(self.pdf(u, v))

but subclasses may override it with a direct analytical expression for numerical stability.

docs.title: Common input preparation
docs.text:
BivariateCopula._prepare_inputs() performs common validation before family-specific mathematics is evaluated.

It:

  1. converts inputs to NumPy floating-point arrays;
  2. broadcasts compatible shapes;
  3. rejects non-finite values;
  4. verifies that all values belong to \([0,1]\).

This logic belongs in the base class because it applies to all copula families.

Family-specific parameter restrictions remain in each subclass.

docs.title: Sample log-likelihood
docs.text:
For a copula parameterized by \(\theta\), the generic sample log-likelihood is

\[ \ell(\theta) = \sum_i \log c_\theta(u_i,v_i). \]

The density itself changes by family; the likelihood construction does not.

This common method is the interface used by the estimation layer:

fit_copula_mle()
        ↓
copula(theta=candidate)
        ↓
log_likelihood(u, v)

The copula class therefore contains the probability model, while pycopula_ml.estimation contains the numerical fitting strategy.

docs.title: Current family support
docs.text:
The package documents these parametric bivariate families:

  • Frank
  • Clayton
  • Gaussian
  • Joe
  • Gumbel-Hougaard
  • Ali-Mikhail-Haq

The fitted copula can also provide mutual information.

docs.title: Parameter estimation
docs.text:
Copula objects are instantiated with known parameters:

copula = FrankCopula(theta=2.0)

When the parameter is unknown, use the estimation package instead:

from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle

result = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(
        (-50.0, -1e-6),
        (1e-6, 50.0),
    ),
)

theta_hat = result.theta

This avoids placing optimizer-specific logic inside FrankCopula.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Dependence measures describe statistical relationships between random variables. For continuous variables, mutual information (MI) measures how far the joint distribution differs from the distribution that would arise under independence.

The pycopula_ml.dependence module uses fitted bivariate copulas to estimate MI and to construct pairwise dependence matrices.

This is a new layer in the package's statistical workflow:

Original observations (X, Y)
            ↓
Marginal CDFs or rank-based pseudo-observations (U, V)
            ↓
Copula parameter estimation (theta_hat)
            ↓
Fitted copula C_theta_hat
            ↓
Model-based mutual information I_C(X; Y)

docs.title: Mutual information
docs.text:
For two jointly continuous random variables, with a well-defined density and finite mutual information,

\[ I(X;Y) =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\!\int_{\mathbb{R}} f_{XY}(x,y) \log\left(\frac{f_{XY}(x,y)}{f_X(x)f_Y(y)}\right) \,dx\,dy. \]

It can also be described as a Kullback--Leibler divergence:

\[ I(X;Y)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{XY}\,\|\,P_X\otimes P_Y). \]

Consequently, MI is nonnegative, is zero exactly under independence, and is symmetric in the two variables. It is not a correlation coefficient and its magnitude is not a percentage. Natural logarithms give values in nats.

When the joint distribution is represented by a copula density \(c(u,v)\), Sklar's theorem yields

\[ \boxed{ I(X;Y)=\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 c(u,v)\log c(u,v)\,du\,dv }. \]

This formulation explains why MI can be obtained directly from a fitted copula without specifying the marginal density formulas again. See Copula-based mutual information.

docs.title: Pairwise dependence in a multivariate sample
docs.text:
Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) contain \(n\) observations and \(d\) features. After fitting a separate bivariate copula for every pair of features, the package can construct:

  • \(\Theta\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\), the fitted copula parameters;
  • \(L\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\), maximized copula log-likelihoods;
  • \(M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\), model-based mutual information in nats.

These are feature-by-feature matrices, not sample-by-sample data matrices. The current implementation uses zero diagonals as placeholders; this does not represent the theoretical MI of a continuous variable with itself.

For supervised classification, the matrices must be estimated separately within each class from training observations belonging to that class. This is analogous to the class-specific dependence learning in R package MLCOPULA 1.1.1; construction of its full probabilistic classifier is a separate stage.

See Pairwise dependence matrices and the Dependence API.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Pairwise MI provides a useful edge-weight candidate for graph construction. However, it does not by itself encode conditional independence, identify causal relationships, build a maximum-spanning tree, or train a graph neural network. Those operations require additional models and algorithms.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The pycopula_ml.estimation package estimates copula parameters after the marginal variables have been transformed to pseudo-observations.

The current workflow is

\[ (X,Y) \rightarrow (U,V) \rightarrow \widehat{\theta}. \]

The responsibilities are deliberately separated:

  • pycopula_ml.marginals transforms original measurements into values on the unit interval;
  • pycopula_ml.copulas evaluates a copula for a supplied parameter;
  • pycopula_ml.estimation searches for the parameter that best explains the observed dependence under the selected copula family.

docs.title: Maximum-likelihood principle
docs.text:
Given paired pseudo-observations

\[ (u_1,v_1),\ldots,(u_n,v_n), \]

and a copula density \(c_\theta\), the sample copula log-likelihood is

\[ \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log c_\theta(u_i,v_i). \]

The estimator seeks

\[ \widehat{\theta} = \operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta} \ell(\theta). \]

The implementation uses a numerical minimizer, so it minimizes the equivalent objective

\[ Q(\theta) = -\ell(\theta). \]

Therefore,

\[ \operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta} Q(\theta) = \operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta} \ell(\theta). \]

docs.title: Why the optimizer is outside the copula classes
docs.text:
A copula object answers questions such as:

copula.cdf(u, v)
copula.pdf(u, v)
copula.logpdf(u, v)
copula.log_likelihood(u, v)

Those operations assume that theta is already known.

Parameter estimation is a different responsibility. It repeatedly creates candidate copulas, evaluates their log-likelihoods, and compares the resulting objective values.

Keeping these responsibilities separate avoids embedding optimization policy inside each copula family.

docs.title: Pseudo-observations
docs.text:
The estimator expects paired one-dimensional arrays satisfying

\[ 0<u_i<1, \qquad 0<v_i<1. \]

The open interval is intentional. Exact values of \(0\) or \(1\) can create singular or numerically unstable log-density evaluations for several copula families.

Original measurements should therefore first be transformed through either:

  • fitted marginal CDFs; or
  • rank-based pseudo-observations.

For example:

from pycopula_ml.marginals import bivariate_pseudo_observations

u, v = bivariate_pseudo_observations(x, y)

docs.title: Likelihood vs pseudo-likelihood
docs.text:
When \(u_i\) and \(v_i\) are observed uniforms under known marginals, maximizing the copula log-likelihood is ordinary maximum-likelihood estimation for the copula parameter.

When \(u_i\) and \(v_i\) are estimated from the same sample, for example by ranks,

\[ u_i=\frac{R_i}{n+1}, \qquad v_i=\frac{S_i}{n+1}, \]

the procedure is commonly described more precisely as a copula pseudo-likelihood or maximum pseudo-likelihood approach.

The current fit_copula_mle() API maximizes the supplied copula log-likelihood in either case. It does not attempt to infer how the pseudo-observations were constructed.

docs.title: Disjoint parameter domains
docs.text:
Some copula families have parameter spaces that are not represented by one closed numerical interval.

For the Frank family,

\[ \theta\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}, \]

while independence is obtained only in the limit

\[ \theta\rightarrow0. \]

Because FrankCopula(theta=0) is not part of the direct parameterization, the estimator can search both sides of zero separately:

result = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(
        (-50.0, -1e-6),
        (1e-6, 50.0),
    ),
)

Each interval is optimized independently and the solution with the largest log-likelihood is selected.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The estimation layer currently supports:

  • one scalar dependence parameter;
  • bounded one-dimensional numerical optimization;
  • one interval or several disjoint intervals;
  • structured optimization results;
  • validation of pseudo-observations and bounds.

It does not yet provide:

  • standard errors or confidence intervals;
  • Hessian-based uncertainty estimates;
  • multivariate parameter optimization;
  • automatic copula-family selection;
  • automatic parameter-domain discovery from a copula class;
  • rank-inversion estimators such as inversion of Kendall's tau.

docs.title: Why marginals are required
docs.text:
Copulas operate on uniform variables, not directly on arbitrary measurements.

Given data \(X\),

\[ X \rightarrow F_X \rightarrow U=F_X(X). \]

The marginals package provides two strategies:

  1. parametric marginal estimation;
  2. empirical/rank-based transformation.

docs.title: Public hierarchy
docs.text:
MarginalModel
├── EmpiricalMarginal
└── ContinuousMarginalModel
    └── ParametricMarginal

docs.title: MarginalModel
docs.text:
Common operations:

  • fit(values)
  • cdf(values)
  • transform(values)

The generic transform applies

\[ u_i=F_X(x_i) \]

and clips exact boundary values to avoid numerical problems in later copula calculations.

docs.title: ContinuousMarginalModel
docs.text:
Adds:

  • pdf(values)
  • logpdf(values)

This interface is appropriate for continuous parametric distributions.

docs.title: Why empirical marginals are separate
docs.text:
An empirical CDF is a step function.

It does not have an ordinary continuous density equivalent to the PDFs provided by SciPy continuous distributions.

Therefore EmpiricalMarginal derives from MarginalModel, not ContinuousMarginalModel.

docs.title: Parametric path
docs.text:
\[ X \rightarrow \widehat F_X^{\text{parametric}} \rightarrow U. \]

Example:

from pycopula_ml.marginals import MarginalSelector

selector = MarginalSelector().fit(x)
u = selector.transform(x)

docs.title: Rank-based path
docs.text:
\[ X \rightarrow R_X \rightarrow U=\frac{R_X}{n+1}. \]

Example:

from pycopula_ml.marginals import pseudo_observations

u = pseudo_observations(x)

The rank-based route avoids assuming a theoretical marginal family.

docs.title: Marginal distributions
docs.text:
For a random variable \(X\), its cumulative distribution function is

\[ F_X(x)=P(X\leq x). \]

For a continuous distribution, its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\frac{dF_X(x)}{dx}. \]

A probability over an interval is obtained by integration:

\[ P(a<X<b) = \int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx. \]

docs.title: Bivariate distribution
docs.text:
For two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\),

\[ F_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X\leq x,\;Y\leq y). \]

If the joint distribution is continuous,

\[ f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{\partial^2F_{X,Y}(x,y)} {\partial x\,\partial y}. \]

docs.title: Probability integral transform
docs.text:
For a continuous variable \(X\),

\[ U=F_X(X) \]

is Uniform on \((0,1)\) under the ideal population model.

Similarly,

\[ V=F_Y(Y). \]

This transformation is the bridge between real-world variables and copulas.

docs.title: Sklar's theorem
docs.text:
For continuous marginal distributions,

\[ F_{X,Y}(x,y) = C(F_X(x),F_Y(y)), \]

or

\[ F_{X,Y}(x,y) = C(u,v). \]

At the density level,

\[ f_{X,Y}(x,y) = c(u,v) f_X(x) f_Y(y). \]

This separates:

  • marginal behavior \(f_X,f_Y\);
  • dependence behavior \(c\).

docs.title: Copula CDF
docs.text:
A bivariate copula is a CDF on the unit square:

\[ C(u,v) = P(U\leq u,\;V\leq v). \]

It satisfies properties including

\[ C(u,0)=0, \] \[ C(0,v)=0, \] \[ C(u,1)=u, \] \[ C(1,v)=v. \]

docs.title: Copula density
docs.text:
For a continuous bivariate copula,

\[ c(u,v) = \frac{\partial^2C(u,v)} {\partial u\,\partial v}. \]

This is what the package names pdf().

docs.title: Log-density
docs.text:
The log-density is

\[ \log c(u,v). \]

It is not a different distribution. It is the same density represented on a logarithmic scale.

The package names this operation logpdf().

docs.title: Likelihood
docs.text:
Given paired observations

\[ (u_1,v_1),\ldots,(u_n,v_n), \]

the copula likelihood for a parameter \(\theta\) is

\[ L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n c_\theta(u_i,v_i). \]

The log-likelihood is

\[ \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log c_\theta(u_i,v_i). \]

This form is preferred computationally because it converts products into sums and reduces numerical underflow.

In the package:

copula.log_likelihood(u, v)

returns this summed log-density for the current copula parameter.

docs.title: Maximum-likelihood estimation
docs.text:
The current scalar estimator solves

\[ \widehat\theta = \operatorname*{argmax}_\theta \ell(\theta). \]

The implementation uses a numerical minimizer on the equivalent objective

\[ Q(\theta) = -\ell(\theta). \]

Therefore,

\[ \widehat\theta = \operatorname*{argmin}_\theta [-\ell(\theta)]. \]

In code:

from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle

result = fit_copula_mle(
    CopulaClass,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(lower, upper),
)

theta_hat = result.theta

docs.title: Why pseudo-observations must stay inside the open unit interval
docs.text:
A copula CDF is defined on

\[ [0,1]^2. \]

However, likelihood estimation uses the copula density and log-density.

For numerical fitting, the estimator requires

\[ 0<u_i<1, \qquad 0<v_i<1. \]

Rank-based pseudo-observations use

\[ u_i=\frac{R_i}{n+1}, \]

which naturally avoids the exact upper boundary \(1\).

docs.title: Copula likelihood and pseudo-likelihood
docs.text:
If the marginal distributions are known and \(U,V\) are exact transformed uniform variables, maximizing

\[ \sum_i\log c_\theta(u_i,v_i) \]

is ordinary copula maximum likelihood.

If the transformations are estimated from the same sample, especially through ranks, the same objective is commonly called a copula pseudo-likelihood.

The current estimator maximizes the supplied copula log-likelihood without trying to determine which marginal-estimation strategy generated \(u\) and \(v\).

docs.title: Disjoint parameter spaces
docs.text:
A numerical optimizer normally searches a continuous bounded interval.

Some copula families require more than one search interval.

For Frank,

\[ \theta\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}. \]

The two regions

\[ \theta<0 \]

and

\[ \theta>0 \]

can therefore be searched independently.

The estimator compares the optimized log-likelihoods from both regions and selects the better result.

docs.title: Parametric bivariate copulas
docs.text:
pycopula_ml.copulas.parametrics contains one-parameter bivariate copula families with a common API:

copula.cdf(u, v)
copula.pdf(u, v)
copula.logpdf(u, v)
copula.log_likelihood(u, v)

The public CDF, PDF, and log-PDF methods share a common parametric interface. Each family provides its own formulas and parameter validation.

docs.title: Independence
docs.text:
The base class treats the family-specific independence parameter explicitly:

\[ C(u,v)=uv,\qquad c(u,v)=1,\qquad \log c(u,v)=0. \]

This avoids numerical indeterminacies in family formulas at independence.

Family Parameter domain used by the library Independence Frank \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\) \(\theta=0\) Clayton \(\theta>-1\) \(\theta=0\) Gaussian \(-1<\theta<1\) \(\theta=0\) Joe \(\theta\ge1\) \(\theta=1\) Gumbel-Hougaard \(\theta\ge1\) \(\theta=1\) Ali-Mikhail-Haq \(-1\le\theta<1\) \(\theta=0\)

For Clayton, the singular endpoint \(\theta=-1\) is intentionally excluded because this package interface assumes an ordinary continuous bivariate density.

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.copulas import (
    AliMikhailHaqCopula,
    ClaytonCopula,
    FrankCopula,
    GaussianCopula,
    GumbelCopula,
    JoeCopula,
)

docs.title: Ali-Mikhail-Haq copula
docs.text:
The Ali-Mikhail-Haq (AMH) copula is

\[ C_\theta(u,v) = \frac{uv}{ 1-\theta(1-u)(1-v) }, \]

with

\[ -1\le\theta<1. \]

Let

\[ d=1-\theta(1-u)(1-v). \]

The density is

\[ c_\theta(u,v) = \frac{ 1+ \theta\left[(1+u)(1+v)-3\right] + \theta^2(1-u)(1-v) }{ d^3 }. \]

docs.title: Independence
docs.text: \[ \theta=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C(u,v)=uv,\qquad c(u,v)=1. \]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.copulas import AliMikhailHaqCopula

copula = AliMikhailHaqCopula(theta=0.5)

cdf = copula.cdf(0.4, 0.7)
pdf = copula.pdf(0.4, 0.7)

docs.title: Clayton copula
docs.text:
The bivariate Clayton copula is

\[ C_\theta(u,v) = \left[ \max\left( u^{-\theta}+v^{-\theta}-1,\, 0 \right) \right]^{-1/\theta}. \]

For the continuous-density implementation in pycopula_ml,

\[ \theta>-1, \]

with \(\theta=0\) interpreted as independence.

The density, where \(s=u^{-\theta}+v^{-\theta}-1>0\), is

\[ c_\theta(u,v) = (1+\theta) (uv)^{-(1+\theta)} s^{-2-1/\theta}. \]

When \(s\le0\), the density is zero.

docs.title: Independence
docs.text:
\[ \theta=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C(u,v)=uv,\qquad c(u,v)=1. \]

The point \(\theta=-1\) is not accepted because it gives the singular lower Fréchet bound rather than an ordinary absolutely continuous density.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.copulas import ClaytonCopula

copula = ClaytonCopula(theta=2.0)

cdf = copula.cdf(0.4, 0.7)
pdf = copula.pdf(0.4, 0.7)
log_pdf = copula.logpdf(0.4, 0.7)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The bivariate Frank copula is

\[ C_\theta(u,v) = -\frac{1}{\theta} \ln \left( 1+ \frac{ (e^{-\theta u}-1)(e^{-\theta v}-1) }{ e^{-\theta}-1 } \right), \]

for

\[ \theta\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}. \]

Positive \(\theta\) represents positive dependence and negative \(\theta\) represents negative dependence.

Independence is obtained as the limiting case

\[ \theta\to0. \]

docs.title: Density
docs.text:
The copula density is

\[ c_\theta(u,v) = \frac{ \theta(1-e^{-\theta})e^{-\theta(u+v)} }{ \left[ (1-e^{-\theta}) - (1-e^{-\theta u})(1-e^{-\theta v}) \right]^2 }. \]

It is obtained from

\[ c_\theta(u,v) = \frac{\partial^2 C_\theta(u,v)} {\partial u\,\partial v}. \]

docs.title: Log-density
docs.text:
The direct log-density can be written as

\[ \log c_\theta(u,v) = \log\left[ \theta(1-e^{-\theta}) \right] -\theta(u+v) - 2\log \left| (1-e^{-\theta}) - (1-e^{-\theta u})(1-e^{-\theta v}) \right|. \]

Direct log-density evaluation is useful because parameter estimation works with sums of log-densities.

docs.title: Sample log-likelihood
docs.text:
For paired pseudo-observations

\[ (u_1,v_1),\ldots,(u_n,v_n), \]

the Frank sample log-likelihood is

\[ \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log c_\theta(u_i,v_i). \]

The class exposes this through:

copula.log_likelihood(u, v)

when copula is a FrankCopula instantiated at a specific candidate \(\theta\).

docs.title: Numerical implementation
docs.text:
The implementation uses NumPy operations such as:

  • np.expm1(x) for \(e^x-1\);
  • np.log1p(x) for \(\log(1+x)\).

These forms improve numerical accuracy near zero.

docs.title: Parameter validation
docs.text:
Although the analytical formula is undefined at theta=0, the implementation handles its continuous independence limit explicitly:

copula = FrankCopula(theta=0.0)
assert copula.cdf(0.3, 0.7) == 0.21
assert copula.pdf(0.3, 0.7) == 1.0
assert copula.logpdf(0.3, 0.7) == 0.0

docs.title: Parameter estimation
docs.text:
When \(\theta\) is unknown, use the estimation layer.

Because Frank excludes exactly zero, search the negative and positive parameter regions separately:

from pycopula_ml.copulas import FrankCopula
from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle


result = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(
        (-50.0, -1e-6),
        (1e-6, 50.0),
    ),
)

theta_hat = result.theta

Internally, each candidate value is evaluated through

\[ -\ell(\theta), \]

and the best successful interval is selected.

The final result reports the statistical log-likelihood directly:

print(result.theta)
print(result.log_likelihood)
print(result.interval)

For Frank:

  • result.theta > 0 indicates positive dependence;
  • result.theta < 0 indicates negative dependence;
  • an estimate numerically close to zero indicates approximate independence.

docs.title: Complete workflow from original data
docs.text:
For raw paired measurements:

from pycopula_ml.copulas import FrankCopula
from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle
from pycopula_ml.marginals import bivariate_pseudo_observations


u, v = bivariate_pseudo_observations(x, y)

result = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(
        (-50.0, -1e-6),
        (1e-6, 50.0),
    ),
)

fitted_copula = FrankCopula(theta=result.theta)

This separates:

x, y
  ↓
marginal/rank transformation
  ↓
u, v
  ↓
MLE
  ↓
theta_hat
  ↓
fitted FrankCopula

docs.title: Direct evaluation example
docs.text:
If \(\theta\) is already known:

from pycopula_ml.copulas import FrankCopula


copula = FrankCopula(theta=2.0)

cdf = copula.cdf(0.3, 0.7)
pdf = copula.pdf(0.3, 0.7)
logpdf = copula.logpdf(0.3, 0.7)

docs.title: Mathematical tests
docs.text:
The test suite checks properties including:

\[ C(u,0)=0, \] \[ C(0,v)=0, \] \[ C(u,1)=u, \] \[ C(1,v)=v, \]

symmetry,

\[ C(u,v)=C(v,u), \]

positive density,

\[ c(u,v)>0, \]

and consistency,

\[ \operatorname{logpdf}(u,v) = \log(\operatorname{pdf}(u,v)). \]

The estimation layer is tested separately so failures in numerical fitting can be distinguished from failures in the Frank probability formulas.

docs.title: Gaussian copula
docs.text:
The bivariate Gaussian copula is constructed from a standard bivariate normal distribution with correlation parameter \(\rho\):

\[ C_\rho(u,v) = \Phi_\rho\left( \Phi^{-1}(u), \Phi^{-1}(v) \right). \]

In the common parametric API, the library stores this parameter as theta, so

\[ \theta=\rho,\qquad -1<\theta<1. \]

Let

\[ z_u=\Phi^{-1}(u),\qquad z_v=\Phi^{-1}(v). \]

The density is

\[ c_\rho(u,v) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \exp\left[ \frac{ 2\rho z_u z_v -\rho^2(z_u^2+z_v^2) }{ 2(1-\rho^2) } \right]. \]

docs.title: Independence
docs.text: \[ \rho=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C(u,v)=uv,\qquad c(u,v)=1. \]

docs.title: Numerical implementation
docs.text: The density and log-density use the analytical formula. The CDF is evaluated using SciPy's bivariate normal CDF.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.copulas import GaussianCopula

copula = GaussianCopula(theta=0.6)

print(copula.rho)
print(copula.pdf(0.4, 0.7))

docs.title: Gumbel-Hougaard copula
docs.text:
The bivariate Gumbel-Hougaard copula is

\[ C_\theta(u,v) = \exp\left[ - \left( (-\log u)^\theta + (-\log v)^\theta \right)^{1/\theta} \right], \]

with

\[ \theta\ge1. \]

Define

\[ x=-\log u,\qquad y=-\log v,\qquad s=x^\theta+y^\theta,\qquad t=s^{1/\theta}. \]

The density is

\[ c_\theta(u,v) = e^{-t} (t+\theta-1) s^{1/\theta-2} (xy)^{\theta-1} (uv)^{-1}. \]

docs.title: Independence
docs.text: \[ \theta=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C(u,v)=uv,\qquad c(u,v)=1. \]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.copulas import GumbelCopula

copula = GumbelCopula(theta=1.8)

cdf = copula.cdf(0.4, 0.7)
pdf = copula.pdf(0.4, 0.7)

docs.title: Joe copula
docs.text:
The bivariate Joe copula is

\[ C_\theta(u,v) = 1- \left[ (1-u)^\theta + (1-v)^\theta - (1-u)^\theta(1-v)^\theta \right]^{1/\theta}, \]

with

\[ \theta\ge1. \]

Define

\[ a=(1-u)^\theta,\qquad b=(1-v)^\theta,\qquad s=a+b-ab. \]

Its density is

\[ c_\theta(u,v) = (1-u)^{\theta-1} (1-v)^{\theta-1} s^{1/\theta-2} \left[ \theta s+ (\theta-1)(1-a)(1-b) \right]. \]

docs.title: Independence
docs.text: \[ \theta=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C(u,v)=uv,\qquad c(u,v)=1. \]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.copulas import JoeCopula

copula = JoeCopula(theta=2.0)

cdf = copula.cdf(0.4, 0.7)
pdf = copula.pdf(0.4, 0.7)

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
pycopula_ml.dependence.mutual_information() evaluates the mutual information implied by an already parameterized, continuous bivariate copula. It does not estimate the copula parameter from data.

For an explanation of the underlying dependence measure, see Dependence measures.

docs.title: Mathematical definition
docs.text:
For jointly continuous \(X\) and \(Y\),

\[ I(X;Y) =\int\!\!\int f_{XY}(x,y) \log\left(\frac{f_{XY}(x,y)}{f_X(x)f_Y(y)}\right) \,dx\,dy. \]

By Sklar's theorem, with \(u=F_X(x)\) and \(v=F_Y(y)\),

\[ f_{XY}(x,y) =c\bigl(F_X(x),F_Y(y)\bigr)f_X(x)f_Y(y). \]

Under the usual regularity conditions, this gives

\[ \boxed{ I(X;Y) =\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 c(u,v)\log c(u,v)\,du\,dv }. \]

For a fitted parametric copula \(c_{\widehat\theta}\), the value returned by the implementation is the model-based quantity

\[ \widehat I_C =\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 c_{\widehat\theta}(u,v) \log c_{\widehat\theta}(u,v)\,du\,dv. \]

It is not necessarily equal to the unknown population MI if the copula family is misspecified or the fitted parameter is imprecise.

Interpretation

A positive MI indicates dependence in the fitted model. MI cannot indicate whether the association is positive or negative, and a value of 0.4 nats does not mean 40% correlation. The measure may exceed one nat.

docs.title: Workflow from original observations
docs.text:
Given paired measurements \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\):

  1. Obtain pseudo-observations \(u_i,v_i\in(0,1)\) from fitted marginal CDFs or rank-based transformations.
  2. Fit a copula parameter \(\widehat\theta\) by maximizing the sample log-likelihood.
  3. Instantiate the copula with the estimated parameter.
  4. Evaluate the mutual-information integral for that fitted copula.

For rank-based pseudo-observations, a common choice is

\[ u_i=\frac{\operatorname{rank}(x_i)}{n+1}, \qquad v_i=\frac{\operatorname{rank}(y_i)}{n+1}. \]

The denominator n + 1 keeps transformed ranks strictly inside the open unit interval. For tied values, an explicit ranking method ensures reproducible pseudo-observations.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata

from pycopula_ml.copulas.parametrics.frank import FrankCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import mutual_information
from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle

x = np.array([10, 15, 20, 25, 30], dtype=float)
y = np.array([20, 35, 30, 45, 50], dtype=float)

u = rankdata(x, method="average") / (len(x) + 1)
v = rankdata(y, method="average") / (len(y) + 1)

fit = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=((-20.0, -1e-4), (1e-4, 20.0)),
)

fitted_copula = FrankCopula(theta=fit.theta)
mi = mutual_information(fitted_copula, order=64)

print(f"theta: {fit.theta:.6f}")
print(f"log-likelihood: {fit.log_likelihood:.6f}")
print(f"mutual information: {mi:.6f} nats")

Illustrative dataset

Five observations are sufficient to demonstrate the API but are generally insufficient for a reliable estimate of dependence. Samples must contain paired observations. Many ties or constant features require additional statistical handling.

fit_copula_mle() operates on pseudo-observations and is documented separately in Maximum-likelihood estimation. The two disjoint intervals shown above avoid the Frank parameter's independence boundary; valid parameter domains depend on the family and its implementation.

docs.title: Numerical integration
docs.text:
For a general fitted continuous copula without a dedicated analytical formula, the implementation performs tensor-product Gauss--Legendre quadrature, using copula.logpdf(u, v) rather than taking the logarithm of an independently calculated PDF:

\[ g(u,v) =\exp\bigl(\log c(u,v)\bigr)\log c(u,v). \]

With \(q\) quadrature nodes and weights on \((0,1)\),

\[ \widehat I_C^{(q)} =\sum_{i=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{q} w_iw_jc(u_i,u_j)\log c(u_i,u_j). \]

The integral requires \(q^2\) log-density evaluations. The quadrature order is controlled by order (default 64, minimum 8 for the numerical branch).

  • The integrand is treated as zero when the density vanishes, using the limit \(c\log c\to0\) as \(c\to0^+\).
  • A nonfinite integrand raises FloatingPointError.
  • A materially negative numerical integral raises ValueError; tiny negative rounding error is clamped to zero.
  • Larger order may improve numerical accuracy but increases computation.

Convergence and tail dependence

A fixed integration order does not guarantee convergence, especially for copulas with strong tail dependence or near-boundary parameters. Compare order=64, 128, and 256 on representative fitted copulas and examine stability. Quadrature integrates the model, not the empirical sample.

docs.title: Gaussian copula: exact result
docs.text:
For a bivariate Gaussian copula with correlation parameter \(\rho\),

\[ \boxed{ I(X;Y)=-\frac{1}{2}\log(1-\rho^2) },\qquad -1<\rho<1. \]

The Gaussian implementation avoids quadrature:

from pycopula_ml.dependence import gaussian_mutual_information

mi = gaussian_mutual_information(rho=0.6)
print(mi)  # approximately 0.2231435513 nats

Passing a GaussianCopula instance to mutual_information() uses the same formula, treating copula.theta as the Gaussian correlation parameter. Consequently, Gaussian correlations of \(0.6\) and \(-0.6\) have identical MI. The order argument does not control the Gaussian closed-form calculation.

docs.title: Mutual information versus log-likelihood
docs.text:
Quantity Definition Role Fitted parameter \(\widehat\theta=\arg\max_\theta\ell(\theta)\) Describes dependence in a specified copula family Sample log-likelihood \(\ell(\widehat\theta)=\sum_k\log c_{\widehat\theta}(u_k,v_k)\) Evaluates the fitted model on the observed pairs Model-based mutual information \(\int_0^1\!\int_0^1c_{\widehat\theta}\log c_{\widehat\theta}\) Measures dependence implied by the fitted copula

The log-likelihood is a sum over observations. MI is an integral over the unit square. They are not interchangeable and need not have the same scale.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
build_weight_matrices() fits one bivariate copula to each distinct pair of feature columns in a matrix of pseudo-observations and returns three pairwise matrices:

  • \(L\): maximized sample copula log-likelihood;
  • \(\Theta\): estimated dependence parameter \(\widehat\theta\);
  • \(M\): model-based mutual information.

docs.title: Input and dimensions
docs.text:
Let \(U\in(0,1)^{n\times d}\) have one row per observation and one column per feature. The function returns arrays in \(\mathbb R^{d\times d}\).

For a pair \(i<j\):

\[ \widehat\theta_{ij} =\underset{\theta}{\arg\max} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \log c_\theta(u_{ki},u_{kj}), \] \[ L_{ij} =\sum_{k=1}^{n} \log c_{\widehat\theta_{ij}}(u_{ki},u_{kj}), \] \[ M_{ij} =\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 c_{\widehat\theta_{ij}}(u,v) \log c_{\widehat\theta_{ij}}(u,v)\,du\,dv. \]

For example, with four features, the fitted MI matrix has the form

\[ M=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & I_{12} & I_{13} & I_{14}\\ I_{12} & 0 & I_{23} & I_{24}\\ I_{13} & I_{23} & 0 & I_{34}\\ I_{14} & I_{24} & I_{34} & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

There are \(d(d-1)/2\) distinct pairs. The implementation copies each value into its transposed position so the three matrices are symmetric, and sets their diagonals to zero.

The diagonal is a software convention

The zeros on the diagonal mean "not estimated" or "no self-edge". They do not assert that \(I(X_i;X_i)=0\), which is false for a nondegenerate continuous variable with itself. The current weight builder assumes symmetric bivariate copula families for pairwise modeling.

docs.title: Pairwise matrix example
docs.text:
The function expects pseudo-observations, not untransformed features. Create them before calling build_weight_matrices():

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata

from pycopula_ml.copulas.parametrics.gaussian import GaussianCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import build_weight_matrices

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
x = rng.normal(size=(120, 4))

u = rankdata(x, axis=0, method="average") / (len(x) + 1)

result = build_weight_matrices(
    u,
    GaussianCopula,
    bounds=(-0.95, 0.95),
    feature_names=("X1", "X2", "X3", "X4"),
    weight_method="mutual_information",
)

print("theta:\n", result.theta)
print("log-likelihood:\n", result.log_likelihood)
print("mutual information (nats):\n", result.mutual_information)
print("selected weights:\n", result.weights)

bounds is passed to the package's existing fit_copula_mle() estimator. The valid domain depends on the copula class; for Frank, its estimation interval is often split around independence. Refer to Maximum-likelihood estimation.

docs.title: One matrix set per class
docs.text:
For supervised learning, let \(y\in\{c_1,\ldots,c_K\}^n\) contain training class labels. For each class \(c\), restrict the training observations to that class, form pseudo-observations within it, and fit the pairwise copulas:

\[ X^{(c)}=\{x_k:y_k=c\}, \qquad U^{(c)}=\operatorname{pobs}(X^{(c)}), \] \[ \bigl(L^{(c)},\Theta^{(c)},M^{(c)}\bigr) =\operatorname{BuildMatrices}(U^{(c)}). \] 
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata

from pycopula_ml.copulas.parametrics.gaussian import GaussianCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import build_weight_matrices

# x_train: array of shape (n_samples, n_features)
# y_train: labels for the same training rows
results_by_class = {}

for label in np.unique(y_train):
    x_class = x_train[y_train == label]
    u_class = rankdata(x_class, axis=0, method="average") / (len(x_class) + 1)

    results_by_class[label] = build_weight_matrices(
        u_class,
        GaussianCopula,
        bounds=(-0.95, 0.95),
        weight_method="mutual_information",
    )

This procedure creates one set of feature-by-feature matrices for each class. The class label itself is not a column of \(U^{(c)}\) and does not form a pair with each feature.

Prevent data leakage

For training/validation/test splits, estimate all marginal transformations, copulas, parameters, and dependence matrices from training data only. Keep preprocessing inside each cross-validation fold to avoid leakage between training and evaluation partitions.

docs.title: Weight selection
docs.text:
The builder exposes weight_method:

Option Returned result.weights Interpretation "mutual_information" result.mutual_information Model-based dependence intensity, in nats "likelihood" result.log_likelihood Maximized copula log-likelihood on the fitting pairs

The two criteria are different. Because log-likelihood is a sample sum, its scale depends on class sample size; avoid treating values from different classes as directly comparable evidence without appropriate normalization or a probabilistic model.

The current builder computes all three matrices regardless of the chosen weight method. Numerical MI integration may therefore add computational cost.

docs.title: Result object
docs.text:
The function returns CopulaWeightMatrices, with fields:

Attribute Type Meaning theta ndarray[d, d] Fitted parameter for every feature pair log_likelihood ndarray[d, d] Maximized copula log-likelihoods mutual_information ndarray[d, d] Copula-based MI values (nats) weights ndarray[d, d] Selected matrix, according to weight_method feature_names tuple[str, ...] Labels of feature columns weight_method str Selected weighting criterion

The result dataclass is frozen, although its underlying NumPy arrays are not necessarily immutable. An input pandas.DataFrame can provide column names when feature_names is not explicitly given.

docs.title: Implementation details and limits
docs.text:
The function processes every distinct pair exactly once, calls fit_copula_mle(), constructs the copula at the fitted theta, evaluates mutual_information(), and fills the three matrices. Data must be a finite, two-dimensional array with at least two rows and columns, with values strictly inside \((0,1)\).

The package currently does not implement in this function:

  • automatic selection of a different copula family per feature pair;
  • maximum-spanning tree or chain extraction;
  • class-conditional likelihood for new observations;
  • model training and class prediction.

The resulting matrices can be passed to graph construction, but they are not a complete classifier.

See the Dependence API, Python examples, and Dependence validation.

docs.title: Public interface
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.estimation import (
    CopulaFitResult,
    fit_copula_mle,
)

fit_copula_mle() estimates a scalar copula dependence parameter by maximizing the copula log-likelihood.

docs.title: Basic workflow
docs.text:
For original paired observations \(x\) and \(y\):

from pycopula_ml.copulas import FrankCopula
from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle
from pycopula_ml.marginals import bivariate_pseudo_observations


u, v = bivariate_pseudo_observations(x, y)

result = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(
        (-50.0, -1e-6),
        (1e-6, 50.0),
    ),
)

print(result.theta)
print(result.log_likelihood)

The workflow is

\[ (x_i,y_i) \rightarrow (u_i,v_i) \rightarrow \ell(\theta) \rightarrow \widehat{\theta}. \]

docs.title: Objective function
docs.text:
For every candidate parameter value, the estimator constructs

copula(theta=theta)

and evaluates

copula.log_likelihood(u, v)

which corresponds to

\[ \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log c_\theta(u_i,v_i). \]

SciPy's scalar optimizer minimizes

\[ -\ell(\theta), \]

and the public result converts the selected objective value back to the maximized log-likelihood.

docs.title: One search interval
docs.text:
For a family whose admissible parameter region can be represented by one bounded interval:

result = fit_copula_mle(
    SomeCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(0.01, 20.0),
)

The lower bound must be strictly smaller than the upper bound.

docs.title: Multiple search intervals
docs.text:
Disjoint domains can be represented by a sequence of intervals:

result = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(
        (-50.0, -1e-6),
        (1e-6, 50.0),
    ),
)

The estimator:

  1. optimizes the negative log-likelihood on each interval;
  2. discards unsuccessful or non-finite solutions;
  3. compares the successful objective values;
  4. returns the solution with the largest log-likelihood.

This removes Frank-specific branching from user scripts.

docs.title: Result object
docs.text:
The return value is a CopulaFitResult.

Important fields are:

result.theta
result.log_likelihood
result.success
result.message
result.nfev
result.n_obs
result.interval
result.raw_result
result.interval_results

docs.title: theta
docs.text:
Maximum-likelihood estimate:

\[ \widehat{\theta}. \]

docs.title: log_likelihood
docs.text:
Maximized value

\[ \ell(\widehat{\theta}). \]

This is returned with the statistical sign convention, even though the underlying optimizer minimizes the negative log-likelihood.

docs.title: interval
docs.text:
The parameter interval that produced the selected optimum.

For a Frank search over both signs, this makes it explicit whether the selected solution came from the negative or positive dependence region.

docs.title: interval_results
docs.text:
Raw SciPy results for every interval searched.

This is mainly useful for diagnostics and development. Most user code should prefer the structured top-level fields.

docs.title: Input validation
docs.text:
The estimator requires u and v to be:

  • one-dimensional;
  • non-empty;
  • equal in shape;
  • finite;
  • strictly inside \((0,1)\).

For example, exact boundary values are rejected:

u = 0
u = 1
v = 0
v = 1

This is stricter than the generic copula CDF domain \([0,1]\) because log-likelihood evaluation is an interior-density calculation.

docs.title: Optimization controls
docs.text:
The current function exposes:

xatol
maxiter

xatol controls the absolute tolerance of the estimated scalar parameter.

maxiter controls the maximum number of optimizer iterations per search interval.

The implementation currently uses SciPy's bounded scalar optimizer internally. This is intentionally hidden behind the pycopula_ml.estimation API.

docs.title: Frank example and association direction
docs.text:
For the bivariate Frank copula:

\[ \widehat{\theta}>0 \]

indicates positive dependence, while

\[ \widehat{\theta}<0 \]

indicates negative dependence.

A fitted value very close to zero indicates approximate independence, even though the direct Frank implementation excludes exactly

\[ \theta=0. \]

Example:

import numpy as np

theta_hat = result.theta

if np.isclose(theta_hat, 0.0, atol=1e-4):
    association = "approximately independent"
elif theta_hat > 0.0:
    association = "positive"
else:
    association = "negative"

docs.title: Numerical failures
docs.text:
If a candidate parameter produces a non-finite log-likelihood, the internal objective treats that candidate as invalid.

If every searched interval fails to produce a finite successful optimization, fit_copula_mle() raises RuntimeError.

This is preferable to silently returning a meaningless parameter estimate.

docs.title: Design note
docs.text:
The user-facing code does not import scipy.optimize.

That separation is intentional:

user code
    ↓
pycopula_ml.estimation.fit_copula_mle
    ↓
SciPy optimization backend

The optimization backend can therefore change later without changing the public estimation workflow.

docs.title: Example: fit Gaussian copulas and construct an MI chain
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata

from pycopula_ml.copulas import GaussianCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import build_weight_matrices
from pycopula_ml.graphs import build_chain_graph

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
z = rng.normal(size=200)
x = np.column_stack(
    [
        z + rng.normal(scale=0.2, size=200),
        rng.normal(size=200),
        z + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=200),
        rng.normal(size=200),
    ]
)

# Training data only: convert each marginal to pseudo-observations in (0,1).
u = rankdata(x, axis=0, method="average") / (len(x) + 1)

weights = build_weight_matrices(
    u,
    GaussianCopula,
    bounds=(-0.98, 0.98),
    weight_method="mutual_information",
    feature_names=("feature_a", "feature_b", "feature_c", "feature_d"),
)
chain = build_chain_graph(weights, method="best")

for edge in chain.edges:
    print(edge.source, "--", edge.target, edge.mutual_information)
print("Chain:", chain.permutation)
print("Total MI (nats):", chain.total_mi)

# Compatible edge indices and attributes for a graph-learning pipeline:
edge_index = chain.edge_index()
edge_attr = chain.edge_attributes()
assert edge_attr.shape[0] == edge_index.shape[1]

The example uses synthetic observations and generic feature names. Fitted copulas describe statistical dependence; the graph constructor selects a path from the mutual-information matrix.

docs.title: Dependence examples
docs.text: These examples use the pycopula_ml.copulas, pycopula_ml.estimation, and pycopula_ml.dependence modules.

docs.title: Example 1: from two measurements to mutual information
docs.text:
This example follows \(X,Y\rightarrow U,V\rightarrow\widehat\theta\rightarrow I(X;Y)\).

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata

from pycopula_ml.copulas.parametrics.frank import FrankCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import mutual_information
from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle

x = np.array([10, 15, 20, 25, 30], dtype=float)
y = np.array([20, 35, 30, 45, 50], dtype=float)

n = len(x)
u = rankdata(x, method="average") / (n + 1)
v = rankdata(y, method="average") / (n + 1)

fit = fit_copula_mle(
    FrankCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=((-20.0, -1e-4), (1e-4, 20.0)),
)

copula = FrankCopula(theta=fit.theta)
mi = mutual_information(copula)

print(f"theta: {fit.theta:.6f}")
print(f"log-likelihood: {fit.log_likelihood:.6f}")
print(f"mutual information: {mi:.6f} nats")

The five observations illustrate the API only; they should not be interpreted as an adequately powered model fit.

docs.title: Example 2: Gaussian closed-form mutual information
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.dependence import gaussian_mutual_information

for rho in (0.0, 0.3, -0.6, 0.6):
    print(rho, gaussian_mutual_information(rho))

The values at rho=-0.6 and rho=0.6 are equal. MI captures the amount of dependence represented by the fitted Gaussian copula, not its direction.

docs.title: Example 3: class-specific matrices with four features
docs.text:
The script below generates three classes with different dependencies between features X1 and X2. For each class it obtains separate \(4\times4\) matrices for theta, log-likelihood, and mutual information.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata

from pycopula_ml.copulas.parametrics.gaussian import GaussianCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import build_weight_matrices

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_per_class = 120

samples = []
labels = []
for label, rho in enumerate((0.1, 0.6, -0.65)):
    z = rng.standard_normal((n_per_class, 4))
    z[:, 1] = rho * z[:, 0] + np.sqrt(1.0 - rho**2) * z[:, 1]
    samples.append(z)
    labels.extend([label] * n_per_class)

x_train = np.vstack(samples)
y_train = np.asarray(labels)

results_by_class = {}
for label in np.unique(y_train):
    x_class = x_train[y_train == label]
    u_class = rankdata(x_class, axis=0, method="average") / (len(x_class) + 1)

    result = build_weight_matrices(
        u_class,
        GaussianCopula,
        bounds=(-0.95, 0.95),
        weight_method="mutual_information",
        feature_names=("X1", "X2", "X3", "X4"),
    )
    results_by_class[label] = result

    print(f"\nClass {label}")
    print("theta:\n", np.round(result.theta, 4))
    print("log-likelihood:\n", np.round(result.log_likelihood, 4))
    print("MI (nats):\n", np.round(result.mutual_information, 4))

The estimated matrices are symmetric with zero diagonals. In this simulation, classes with larger absolute pairwise correlations should generally have higher MI for the (X1, X2) pair, despite differing signs.

docs.title: Example 4: display MI as a labeled matrix
docs.text:
The following fragment continues Example 3:

import pandas as pd

result = results_by_class[0]
mi_table = pd.DataFrame(
    result.mutual_information,
    index=result.feature_names,
    columns=result.feature_names,
)
print(mi_table.round(4))

Pandas is only required for tabular display, not for the dependence calculations.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Run the companion dependence tests with:

python -m pytest tests/dependence -v

See Dependence validation for the test coverage and recommended statistical checks.

docs.title: Example: exact maximum-MI spanning tree
docs.text:
This example illustrates how a minimum spanning tree algorithm applied to negative mutual information maximizes the retained information.

import numpy as np

from pycopula_ml.graphs import build_chain_graph, build_mst_graph

mi = np.array(
    [
        [0, 9, 8, 7],
        [9, 0, 1, 1],
        [8, 1, 0, 1],
        [7, 1, 1, 0],
    ],
    dtype=float,
)

labels = ["central", "left", "middle", "right"]

mst = build_mst_graph(mi, feature_names=labels)
chain = build_chain_graph(mi, method="best", feature_names=labels)

print(mst.edge_indices)  # ((0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3))
print(mst.total_mi)  # 24.0
print(mst.total_cost)  # -24.0
print(chain.total_mi)  # Less than 24: a chain cannot branch
print(mst.adjacency_matrix(weighted=False))

# Matrices for downstream graph-learning code:
edge_index = mst.edge_index()  # (2, 6), both directions
edge_attributes = mst.edge_attributes()  # (6, 1), positive MI values

docs.title: Connecting a CopulaWeightMatrices result
docs.text:
After computing pseudo-observations and fitting bivariate copulas with build_weight_matrices, you may pass the result object directly:

from pycopula_ml.graphs import build_mst_graph

# `matrices` is a CopulaWeightMatrices result computed earlier.
mst = build_mst_graph(matrices)

build_mst_graph extracts the .mutual_information matrix even if matrices.weight_method == "likelihood". You should not negate the MI matrix before passing it; -MI is an internal optimization cost.

Note that an optimal tree can have maximum degree greater than two; use chain construction if your model explicitly requires a path.
