docs.title: Fit a bivariate copula
docs.text:
The copula fitting functions expect paired observations in the open unit interval. Convert a pair of continuous feature columns to rank-based pseudo-observations before estimating dependence.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata

from pycopula_ml.copulas import GaussianCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import mutual_information
from pycopula_ml.estimation import fit_copula_mle

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
x = rng.normal(size=200)
y = 0.7 * x + rng.normal(scale=0.7, size=200)

u = rankdata(x, method="average") / (len(x) + 1)
v = rankdata(y, method="average") / (len(y) + 1)

fit = fit_copula_mle(
    GaussianCopula,
    u,
    v,
    bounds=(-0.98, 0.98),
)

copula = GaussianCopula(theta=fit.theta)
print(f"Estimated parameter: {fit.theta:.4f}")
print(f"Mutual information: {mutual_information(copula):.4f} nats")

docs.title: Build a feature-dependence graph
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import rankdata

from pycopula_ml.copulas import GaussianCopula
from pycopula_ml.dependence import build_weight_matrices
from pycopula_ml.graphs import build_mst_graph

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
features = rng.normal(size=(200, 4))
u = rankdata(features, axis=0, method="average") / (len(features) + 1)

matrices = build_weight_matrices(
    u,
    GaussianCopula,
    bounds=(-0.98, 0.98),
    feature_names=("feature_a", "feature_b", "feature_c", "feature_d"),
)
graph = build_mst_graph(matrices)

print(graph.total_mi)
print(graph.edge_indices)

For class-specific dependence models, fit marginal transforms, copulas, and feature graphs exclusively on each class's training data. The graph is a structural component; it is not itself a classifier.

Continue with the dependence examples or the API reference.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Given a symmetric, nonnegative pairwise mutual-information matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\), select an open path visiting all features exactly once and maximizing

\[ \max_{\pi\in S_d} \sum_{k=1}^{d-1}M_{\pi_k,\pi_{k+1}}. \]

The chain has \(d-1\) undirected edges and does not branch. All weights are measured in nats. Finding the global optimum is computationally hard; the supported algorithms are heuristics, not exact solvers.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.graphs import build_chain_graph

chain = build_chain_graph(mi_matrix, method="best")

mi_matrix may be a NumPy array or a CopulaWeightMatrices result. In the latter case, the builder extracts .mutual_information rather than the configurable .weights property.

Member Meaning order Original zero-based feature indices in chain order permutation Feature names in chain order edges Named edges and their mutual-information weights total_mi Sum of the selected weights (nats) method Selected algorithm ("greedy" or "tsp") adjacency_matrix(weighted=True) Symmetric weighted adjacency edge_index(bidirectional=True) NumPy indices for graph algorithms edge_attributes(bidirectional=True) Edge weights aligned with indices

The input must be square, finite, symmetric, have a zero diagonal, and have nonnegative entries. Feature names must be unique when supplied.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
• "greedy": Start from the strongest pair and extend either endpoint with the strongest available connection.
  • "tsp": Use multiple nearest-neighbor starts and 2-opt improvements to construct a high-scoring open path.
  • "best": Run both heuristics and return the higher-scoring path.

A chain differs from a maximum-weight spanning tree, which may have branching vertices. If an algorithm needs the unweighted topology, use adjacency_matrix(weighted=False) to preserve zero-weight edges.

docs.title: Use with classification data
docs.text:
Estimate marginal transformations and dependence on training records only. For class-specific models, compute separate matrices within each training class. The resulting chain represents statistical feature dependence; it neither proves causality nor performs class prediction.

See the chain example.

docs.title: Problem and terminology
docs.text:
Given a symmetric pairwise mutual-information matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\), select a set of \(d-1\) undirected edges that connects all \(d\) variables, has no cycles, and maximizes the sum of selected mutual-information weights:

\[ T^* = \underset{T\text{ spanning tree}}{\arg\max} \sum_{(i,j)\in E(T)} M_{ij}. \]

Here \(M_{ij}=I(X_i;X_j)\geq 0\) is measured in nats. This is a maximum-weight spanning tree, obtained using a minimum spanning tree algorithm on transformed costs:

\[ C_{ij} = -M_{ij}, \qquad \underset{T}{\arg\min}\sum_{(i,j)\in E(T)}C_{ij} = \underset{T}{\arg\max}\sum_{(i,j)\in E(T)}M_{ij}. \]

Important: callers provide the positive MI matrix. The Python implementation multiplies each weight by -1 internally. Do not negate the input yourself. The result reports both total_mi (maximized) and total_cost (minimized, equal to -total_mi).

A spanning tree is not a Hamiltonian chain. Trees can branch; a chain requires all vertices to have degree at most two. The maximum-MI tree is therefore never worse in total selected MI than the optimum MI chain on the same matrix, because every chain is also a tree.

docs.title: Exact algorithm: Kruskal on negative MI
docs.text:
1. Validate that the matrix is symmetric, finite, square, has zero diagonal, and contains nonnegative MI values.
  2. Create all unordered candidate pairs \((i,j)\) with \(i<j\).
  3. Set the cost of every pair to \(-M_{ij}\) and sort ascending by cost, breaking ties by feature indices \((i,j)\).
  4. Traverse the sorted pairs. Keep an edge only if it connects two previously separate components (union–find / disjoint-set structure).
  5. Stop after selecting exactly \(d-1\) edges.

Kruskal solves the spanning-tree objective globally for the supplied weights, unlike the greedy and TSP-inspired algorithms used for the more constrained chain problem. If multiple trees have the same optimum score, our index-based tie-breaking makes results deterministic; it is not a statement about the uniqueness of the statistical dependence structure.

For a dense matrix, creating and sorting all pairs takes \(O(d^2\log d)\) time and \(O(d^2)\) additional memory. This excludes the potentially more expensive work of estimating copulas and calculating their MI values.

docs.title: API and example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from pycopula_ml.graphs import build_mst_graph

mi = np.array(
    [
        [0, 1, 8, 2],
        [1, 0, 3, 9],
        [8, 3, 0, 7],
        [2, 9, 7, 0],
    ],
    dtype=float,
)

mst = build_mst_graph(mi, feature_names=["A", "B", "C", "D"])

print(mst.edge_indices)  # ((1, 3), (0, 2), (2, 3))
print(mst.total_mi)  # 24.0
print(mst.total_cost)  # -24.0
print(mst.edge_weights)  # [9. 8. 7.]
print(mst.edge_costs)  # [-9. -8. -7.]

adjacency = mst.adjacency_matrix()
edge_index = mst.edge_index()
edge_attr = mst.edge_attributes()

This matrix happens to give the same topology as the example chain: A--C--D--B, but that coincidence is not guaranteed.

For example, if one variable has MI 9, 8, and 7 with three other variables, and all three leaf-to-leaf MI values are 1, the optimal tree is a star with score 24, whereas a chain cannot use all three central edges.

docs.title: Input and output contracts
docs.text:
build_mst_graph(mi_matrix, *, feature_names=None) accepts either a numpy-compatible matrix or a CopulaWeightMatrices object. In the latter case it always reads .mutual_information, not .weights (which can contain pairwise log-likelihoods instead).

SpanningTreeGraph contains:

Member Interpretation feature_names Original column order and labels edge_indices Selected undirected pairs (i,j) with i < j edges SpanningTreeEdge(source, target, mutual_information) edge_weights Positive MI on selected edges, in nats edge_costs Negative MI used to choose the tree total_mi Sum of the MI values; maximized total_cost Sum of negative MI costs; minimized adjacency_matrix(weighted=True) Symmetric MI-weighted adjacency adjacency_matrix(weighted=False) Binary topology, including zero-MI edges edge_index(bidirectional=True) (2, 2(d-1)) edge-index array edge_attributes(bidirectional=True) (2(d-1), 1) MI features aligned with edge-index columns

For interoperability with graph-processing code, undirected edges appear in both directions in edge_index() by default. They still represent one mathematical edge per pair. edge_attributes() follows the same order. No separate graph-learning framework is required.

docs.title: Zero-valued MI
docs.text: Zero MI means zero statistical weight, not "edge forbidden". The input is a complete candidate graph. If all MI values are zero, the algorithm returns a valid spanning tree with \(d-1\) edges and a total MI of zero. Use adjacency_matrix(weighted=False) to inspect the selected topology: zero-weight edges cannot be distinguished from absent edges in the weighted adjacency matrix.

docs.title: Connection to the copula pipeline
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.graphs import build_mst_graph

# `matrices` is a CopulaWeightMatrices result computed earlier.
mst = build_mst_graph(matrices)

The copulas and marginal transformations are fitted before MST selection. In a supervised classifier, fit these transformations on training data only, and avoid leakage from validation/test data.

A maximum-MI spanning tree provides a feature-dependence topology. Its edges do not imply causality or prove conditional independence in the original data. Model-based MI inherits the uncertainty of the fitted copulas and marginal transformations.

See also MST usage example and graph validation.

docs.title: Empirical CDF
docs.text:
For observations

\[ X_1,\ldots,X_n, \]

the empirical cumulative distribution function is

\[ \widehat F_n(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf 1(X_i\leq x). \]

EmpiricalMarginal stores the sample and evaluates this step function efficiently using sorted observations and numpy.searchsorted.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from pycopula_ml.marginals import EmpiricalMarginal


x = np.array([10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0])

marginal = EmpiricalMarginal().fit(x)

print(marginal.cdf([5.0, 10.0, 25.0, 40.0]))

Expected ECDF values are

\[ [0,\;0.25,\;0.5,\;1]. \]

docs.title: Pseudo-observations
docs.text:
For copula estimation, the package also provides rank-based pseudo-observations:

\[ u_i = \frac{R_i}{n+1}. \]

The \(n+1\) denominator keeps the transformed observations away from the exact value \(1\).

Example:

from pycopula_ml.marginals import pseudo_observations

u = pseudo_observations(x)

docs.title: Ties
docs.text:
The default ranking method is average rank.

For

\[ [10,20,20,40], \]

the two tied values receive the same average rank.

Alternative ranking behavior can be requested through the ties argument where supported by scipy.stats.rankdata.

docs.title: Bivariate pseudo-observations
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.marginals import (
    bivariate_pseudo_observations,
)

u, v = bivariate_pseudo_observations(x, y)

Both samples must contain the same number of observations.

Each marginal is ranked independently.

docs.title: ECDF vs pseudo-observations
docs.text:
These are related but not identical.

For the largest fitted observation,

\[ \widehat F_n(x_{\max})=1. \]

Rank-based pseudo-observations instead yield

\[ u_{\max} = \frac{n}{n+1} <1. \]

For copula pseudo-likelihood estimation, the rank transformation is usually the more direct tool.

docs.title: MarginalSelector
docs.text:
MarginalSelector fits several candidate parametric distributions and ranks successful fits.

Default candidates currently include:

  • Normal;
  • Gamma;
  • Lognormal;
  • Weibull;
  • Exponential.

docs.title: Selection criteria
docs.text:
Supported criteria:

aic
bic
ks

The selected model minimizes the configured quantity.

docs.title: AIC
docs.text:
\[ AIC=2k-2\ell. \]

Lower is better.

docs.title: BIC
docs.text:
\[ BIC=k\log n-2\ell. \]

Lower is better.

docs.title: KS statistic
docs.text:
\[ D = \sup_x \left| F_n(x)-F(x) \right|. \]

Lower is better.

docs.title: Why the KS p-value is not the default selector
docs.text:
The classical one-sample KS p-value assumes a fully specified theoretical distribution.

When the same sample is used both to estimate distribution parameters and to compute the KS test, the standard p-value is no longer formally calibrated in the usual way.

The package therefore stores it as an exploratory diagnostic rather than using it as the default selection rule.

docs.title: Selected does not mean true
docs.text:
The package uses the name

selected_model_

rather than interpreting the model as the true generating distribution.

The meaning is:

preferred model among the supplied candidate set under the configured selection criterion.

Aliases such as best_model_ may exist for convenience, but selected_model_ is statistically more precise.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pycopula_ml.marginals import MarginalSelector


selector = MarginalSelector(
    criterion="aic",
)

selector.fit(x)

print(selector.summary())

model = selector.selected_model_
u = selector.transform(x)

docs.title: Custom candidates
docs.text:
from scipy.stats import gamma, lognorm, norm

from pycopula_ml.marginals import (
    MarginalCandidate,
    MarginalSelector,
)


candidates = [
    MarginalCandidate(
        name="normal",
        distribution=norm,
    ),
    MarginalCandidate(
        name="gamma",
        distribution=gamma,
        fit_kwargs={"floc": 0.0},
    ),
    MarginalCandidate(
        name="lognormal",
        distribution=lognorm,
        fit_kwargs={"floc": 0.0},
    ),
]

selector = MarginalSelector(
    candidates=candidates,
    criterion="aic",
)

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text:
The selector can warn about:

  • small samples;
  • fitted support boundaries close to observed extrema;
  • candidate fitting failures.

These warnings are diagnostic. They do not automatically invalidate a model.

docs.title: Small samples
docs.text:
Automatic distribution selection is especially unstable when the sample is very small relative to the number of fitted parameters.

The package should therefore report rather than hide this uncertainty.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ParametricMarginal wraps continuous distributions from scipy.stats.

The package does not reimplement Normal, Gamma, Lognormal, Weibull, or Exponential distributions.

SciPy remains responsible for:

  • parameter fitting;
  • PDF evaluation;
  • log-PDF evaluation;
  • CDF evaluation;
  • distribution support.

pycopula-ml adds a consistent interface and diagnostics needed by the copula workflow.

docs.title: Example: Normal
docs.text:
from scipy.stats import norm

from pycopula_ml.marginals import ParametricMarginal


marginal = ParametricMarginal(
    norm,
    name="normal",
)

marginal.fit(x)

u = marginal.transform(x)

For a Normal model, SciPy uses

\[ \mu=\text{loc}, \qquad \sigma=\text{scale}. \]

docs.title: Example: Gamma with fixed location
docs.text:
from scipy.stats import gamma

from pycopula_ml.marginals import ParametricMarginal


marginal = ParametricMarginal(
    gamma,
    name="gamma",
    fit_kwargs={
        "floc": 0.0,
    },
)

marginal.fit(x)

Fixing loc=0 is a modeling assumption and should only be used when the variable's support justifies it.

docs.title: Fit result
docs.text:
A successful fit stores a MarginalFitResult containing:

  • distribution name;
  • fitted parameters;
  • sample size;
  • number of free parameters;
  • log-likelihood;
  • AIC;
  • BIC;
  • KS statistic;
  • exploratory KS p-value.

docs.title: Information criteria
docs.text:
For \(k\) free parameters,

\[ AIC = 2k-2\ell, \]

and

\[ BIC = k\log n-2\ell. \]

Lower values are preferred within the candidate set.

Fixed parameters are excluded from the free-parameter count when possible.

docs.title: Probability integral transform
docs.text:
After fitting,

u = marginal.transform(x)

computes

\[ u_i=\widehat F_X(x_i) \]

and clips numerical boundaries into the open unit interval.

docs.title: Copula model selection
docs.text:
The model_selection package exposes three distinct responsibilities:

  1. aic(log_likelihood, n_parameters): Akaike's information criterion.
  2. bic(log_likelihood, n_parameters, n_observations): Bayesian information criterion.
  3. copula_selector(candidates, u, v, criterion="bic"): estimate and rank several bivariate copula families on identical paired observations.

For \(n\) paired observations and \(k\) fitted parameters,

\[ \mathrm{AIC} = 2k - 2\ell(\hat\theta),\qquad \mathrm{BIC} = k\ln(n) - 2\ell(\hat\theta). \] 
from pycopula_ml.copulas import FrankCopula, GaussianCopula
from pycopula_ml.model_selection import copula_selector

candidate_copulas = {
    FrankCopula: (-8.0, 8.0),
    GaussianCopula: (-0.98, 0.98),
}
result = copula_selector(candidate_copulas, u, v, criterion="bic")
print(result.selected.name, result.selected.theta)

The vectors u and v must represent the same observations across candidate models. Do not use test-set observations for fitting or ranking. CopulaSelectionResult.candidates contains ordered CopulaCriteria values including family, theta, log-likelihood, AIC and BIC.

The implementation is intentionally separate from marginal selection and the MI-driven graph constructor. For tests, see tests/model_selection/test_criteria.py and test_selector.py.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The following resources provide background on the statistical methods used by this library. They are not required for installation.

docs.title: Copulas and bivariate distributions
docs.text:
Balakrishnan, N., & Lai, C.-D. (2009). Continuous Bivariate Distributions (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/b101765

Nelsen, R. B. (2006). An Introduction to Copulas (2nd ed.). Springer.

docs.title: Information theory
docs.text: Cover, T. M., & Thomas, J. A. (2006). Elements of Information Theory (2nd ed.). Wiley.

docs.title: Numerical computation
docs.text:
SciPy documentation: https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/

NumPy documentation: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/

The library uses SciPy statistical distributions and numerical optimization. Its mutual-information routines use analytical expressions where available and numerical integration for other supported continuous copulas.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
Where present in the repository, tests in tests/dependence/ should cover:

  1. Exact Gaussian mutual information, including independence and sign symmetry.
  2. Domain validation for Gaussian correlation parameters.
  3. Numerical integration of copula-based mutual information.
  4. Zero mutual information under independence.
  5. Shape, symmetry, and diagonal conventions of pairwise matrices.
  6. Invalid pseudo-observations, nonfinite values, and fitting failures.
python -m pytest tests/dependence -v

docs.title: Statistical checks
docs.text:
• Check family-specific mutual information at valid reference parameters.
  • Compare quadrature orders (for example, 64, 128, and 256) and report convergence differences when dependence is strong.
  • Separate estimation error from numerical integration error.
  • Test tied ranks, constant features, and insufficient class sample sizes.
  • Confirm that class-specific transformations do not access validation or test data.
  • Keep random seeds fixed in reproducible simulations.

Numerical quadrature can differ slightly from reference values even when the underlying copula parameter is identical. Record tolerances and floating- point assumptions in statistical regression tests.

docs.title: Estimation testing and statistical validation
docs.text:
Parameter estimation requires more than one kind of test.

A deterministic software test and a Monte Carlo validation experiment answer different questions and should not be mixed.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
The estimation unit tests verify the behavior of the optimization code itself.

A useful deterministic test defines a synthetic log-likelihood with a known maximum, for example

\[ \ell(\theta) = -(\theta-2.5)^2. \]

Its exact optimum is

\[ \widehat{\theta}=2.5. \]

The optimizer can therefore be tested without depending on the Frank implementation.

Current estimation unit tests should cover:

  • recovery of a known deterministic maximum;
  • selection of the best result across disjoint intervals;
  • rejection of values outside \((0,1)\);
  • rejection of mismatched sample shapes;
  • rejection of reversed parameter bounds.

Run them with:

python -m pytest tests/estimation -v

These tests belong in tests/ because they are deterministic, fast, and suitable for continuous integration.

docs.title: Integration tests
docs.text:
An integration test answers a broader question:

Do the marginal transformation, copula implementation, and estimation layer work correctly together?

A representative integration path is:

x, y
  ↓
bivariate_pseudo_observations()
  ↓
u, v
  ↓
FrankCopula
  ↓
fit_copula_mle()
  ↓
theta_hat

Integration tests should use fixed data and deterministic expected behavior so they remain stable in CI.

At the current stage, this is the recommended next testing layer after the estimation unit tests.

docs.title: Statistical validation
docs.text:
A Monte Carlo experiment answers a statistical question rather than a software unit-test question.

For a known generating parameter,

\[ \theta_{\text{true}}, \]

generate repeated samples

\[ (U_i,V_i) \sim C_{\text{Frank}}(\theta_{\text{true}}) \]

and estimate

\[ \widehat{\theta} \]

for each sample.

The validation script can then study the sampling behavior of the estimator.

This belongs under a path such as:

scripts/validation/

rather than the core unit-test suite.

docs.title: Bias
docs.text:
For \(R\) repeated experiments,

\[ \operatorname{Bias} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^{R} (\widehat{\theta}_r-\theta_{\text{true}}). \]

Bias measures systematic directional error.

  • positive bias: tendency to overestimate;
  • negative bias: tendency to underestimate;
  • bias near zero: no strong systematic direction in the experiment.

docs.title: MAE
docs.text:
The mean absolute error is

\[ MAE = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^{R} \left| \widehat{\theta}_r-\theta_{\text{true}} \right|. \]

It measures the average magnitude of the estimation error.

Unlike bias, positive and negative errors do not cancel.

docs.title: RMSE
docs.text:
The root mean squared error is

\[ RMSE = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^{R} (\widehat{\theta}_r-\theta_{\text{true}})^2 }. \]

RMSE gives greater weight to unusually large errors than MAE.

Typically,

\[ RMSE\geq MAE. \]

docs.title: Recommended validation grid
docs.text:
A stronger statistical validation should vary both dependence strength and sample size.

For example:

theta_true = 1, 2, 5, 10
n          = 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000

For each configuration, repeat the experiment many times and record:

  • mean \(\widehat{\theta}\);
  • standard deviation of \(\widehat{\theta}\);
  • bias;
  • MAE;
  • RMSE;
  • optimizer success rate.

The expected large-sample behavior is that estimation error decreases as the sample size grows.

This is evidence about the statistical estimator. It is not a replacement for deterministic unit tests.

docs.title: Graph-construction tests
docs.text:
Run applicable test modules from the repository root:

python -m pytest tests/graphs -v
python -m pytest --cov=pycopula_ml --cov-report=term-missing

docs.title: Expected properties
docs.text:
• A connected spanning tree or chain over all feature vertices.
  • Exactly d - 1 selected undirected edges.
  • No duplicate vertices, cycles, or invalid edge indices.
  • Deterministic tie-breaking and no in-place mutation of input matrices.
  • Input validation for symmetry, finiteness, nonnegativity, and diagonals.
  • Correct handling of zero-weight edges and feature names.
  • Agreement between edge indices, attributes, and adjacency matrices.
  • Exact MST score against small hand-checkable examples.
  • Chain scores verified without claiming global optimality.

For end-to-end checks, compute pseudo-observations and pairwise copula mutual information before constructing a graph. Verify that all fitting uses the training partition only.
